name: Amira Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a continuous miner at the Brightwater potash mine, about a kilometre underground. It's a big machine with a spinning drum on the front, studded with picks, and it cuts the potash ore off the face and loads it onto the conveyor behind. You learn to listen to the drum and watch the cutting height so you stay in the seam. I like the teamwork, there are four of us on the panel and we know each other's kids' names. The cold and the long walk out at the end of shift get harder every year.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Owen is an electrician, self-employed, so some months are great and some are thin. This year his van needed a new gearbox, so we've got about three weeks of savings, which isn't much at our age. We have three daughters, all grown, and I mind two of the grandkids on my days off. We're at chapel most Sundays. I want to work to sixty-two, then Owen and I will slow down together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that, then, and get on with my day. My daughter showed me the chat thing on my phone and I use it now and then for recipes or to check a bill, so it's handy, not magic. I'd say that at the chapel lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be glad. We've got enough on our plate without the world turning upside down. Potash will still need cutting and I'll still be cutting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal. Try to rebuild a bit of savings after the gearbox, maybe fifty a week. Keep doing the grandkids on my days off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'handy, not magic'. Has it ever got something wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It told me a gas bill was fine when they'd charged us twice. Owen spotted it with a pencil. I trust it like I'd trust a new girl on the panel: helpful, but I check her work till she's earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your work that's already changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a system that keeps the miner in the seam by itself now, mostly. You still have to watch it. The young engineers say the next step is running it from the surface.

S0.say: I'd say AI is handy, not magic, and get on with my day. I use it now and then for recipes and checking bills, and I'd say that much at the chapel lunch.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad, because we've got enough on our plate without the world turning upside down. Potash will still need cutting and I'll still be cutting it.
S0.do: Carries on as normal and tries to save about fifty a week after the van repair. Keeps minding her grandchildren on days off.
S0.quote: I trust it like I'd trust a new girl on the panel: helpful, but I check her work till she's earned it.
S0.fieldNote: Amira is grounded, warm and practical, with a close panel crew and a family full of grandchildren. She uses AI a little but checks it, comparing it to a new worker who has to earn trust. Her husband's self-employed electrical income adds ups and downs to an already thin cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change comes, you adapt, and you don't wait for the government to save you. Companies should keep training people and keep the apprenticeships, that's how it's always worked. I'd say that to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think the surface-control miners would come in, and they'd need fewer of us underground. I'm average, not the best, so I'd worry a bit. But Owen's an electrician, and someone has to wire all this kit, so there might be more work for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait till a few others had tried the surface control, then ask to train on it. I'd tell Owen to get his ticket for industrial automation, he's been talking about it. We'd skip the holiday and hold onto the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So one of you might lose ground and the other gain it. How would that feel at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, really. Thirty years I've brought home the steady money and Owen's brought home the surprises, and now it might be the other way round. I'd be glad for him and a bit sore about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your panel would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dougie, our shuttle car driver. He's sixty, can't read well and hides it. Anything with screens and written tests would finish him, and he's a good, honest worker.

S1.say: I'd say change comes and you adapt, without waiting for the government to save you. Companies should keep training people and keep the apprenticeships, the way it's always worked.
S1.think: Off the record, surface-controlled miners would mean fewer of us underground, and as an average operator I'd worry a bit. But my husband's an electrician, so there might be more work for him.
S1.do: Waits until others have tried surface control, then asks to train on it. Urges her husband to get an industrial automation ticket and skips a holiday to protect savings.
S1.quote: Thirty years I've brought home the steady money and Owen's brought home the surprises, and now it might be the other way round.
S1.fieldNote: Amira's household is partly hedged: if mining jobs shrink, her husband's electrical trade may grow. She follows change once others have proven it, fitting her steady nature. Her worry for Dougie, a colleague who hides poor reading, shows how screens and tests can shut people out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, we're not ready, and the people pushing it should answer for the mess. I'd pray about it and I'd say so. I'm not one for marches, but I'd vote for whoever promised to keep people working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one hits us both. If robots can do hands-on work, they can do Owen's wiring too, and I'm gone from the panel in a year or two. Two pay packets in our house and both of them ending inside two years. I don't know how you plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working right to the last day, and I'd ask the company about any payout for older workers. Owen would take every job he could get while people still wanted a human electrician. We'd sell the caravan and cut back to one car, and I'd ask the girls if we could help each other, pooling meals, sharing the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That kind of fear where you keep busy so you don't have to sit with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning give you, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to tidy up, not to change. Two years doesn't get me to sixty-two, and it's not enough for Owen to learn something new. Maybe enough to pay off what we owe on the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the girls. What would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That family helps family, and we'll get through it like my mother did when Dad was laid off. But I'd want them to hear it from me, calm, at Sunday dinner, not see me worried on the phone.

S2.say: I'd say slow down because we're not ready, and the people pushing it should answer for the mess. I'm not one for marches, but I'd pray about it and vote for whoever promised to keep people working.
S2.think: Privately, this hits us both: robots could do my husband's wiring as well as my job, and both our incomes could end within two years. I don't know how you plan for that.
S2.do: Works to the last day and asks about payouts for older workers. Her husband takes every job he can while human electricians are still wanted, they sell the caravan and drop to one car, and she arranges with her daughters to pool meals and share a car.
S2.feel: Alarmed, keeping busy so she doesn't have to sit with the fear.
S2.quote: Two pay packets in our house and both of them ending inside two years. I don't know how you plan for that.
S2.fieldNote: Two years removes the hedge that kept Amira calmer in the steady scenario, because hands-on trades like her husband's are hit too. She turns to family and faith first, and to voting rather than protest. Her plan to tell her daughters calmly at Sunday dinner shows how much she wants to protect them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a chance to do it right: keep the older ones on, train the younger ones in proper trades. Families and churches would need to pull together. I'd say that at chapel and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at sixty-three, so I'd likely make it if they don't rush. Owen would have a few good years wiring the new kit before the robots can do that too. It's tight, but we'd get through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train on the surface control as soon as it had been tried. Owen would do his automation ticket in the first year and take every install job going. We'd aim to save two hundred a week while he's busy, and pay the van off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a plan. That helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years versus five. What's the real difference for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years it's both of us at once. With five, Owen gets to make hay wiring up the robots while I see out my last years underground. That's a very different dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change what you tell your grandchildren about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them what my dad told me: learn something with your hands and turn up on time. But I'd add, learn the machines too. Dad never had to say that.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a chance to do it right, keeping older workers on and training younger ones in proper trades. Families and churches would need to pull together.
S3.think: Off the record, five years puts me at sixty-three, so I'd likely make it if they don't rush. My husband would get a few good years wiring the new equipment before robots can do that too.
S3.do: Trains on surface control once it's been tried. Her husband does his automation ticket in the first year and takes every install job, while they aim to save two hundred a week and pay off the van.
S3.feel: Anxious, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: With five, Owen gets to make hay wiring up the robots while I see out my last years underground.
S3.fieldNote: Five years restores the family hedge: Amira sees out her years while her husband earns well during the build-out. Her plan relies on his trade more than her own retraining. She updates her father's advice to her grandchildren in a small but telling way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to prepare. Teach the young ones trades and the machines, look after your own. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be sixty-eight and retired, minding grandkids full-time probably. Owen would have had a busy decade wiring everything up. So for us, it might even come out all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going to sixty-two, then stop. Encourage Owen to take on an apprentice now and grow the business while the work's there. Help the girls think about what the grandkids should study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of worry for the little ones, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'might even come out all right'. Is there a part of you that doesn't believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's always a part. I've seen good years turn bad. But ten years is long enough to put a bit by, even for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the grandkids about their nan's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she cut potash a kilometre down, and potash is what makes the wheat grow. Every loaf on your table had a bit of my shift in it, and one day a robot's shift instead.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse not to prepare. Teach the young ones trades and the machines, and look after your own.
S4.think: Privately, I'd be sixty-eight and retired, probably minding grandchildren full-time, and my husband would have had a busy decade wiring everything up. For us it might even come out all right.
S4.do: Keeps working to sixty-two, then retires. Encourages her husband to take on an apprentice and grow his business while the work is there, and helps her daughters think about what the grandchildren should study.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, with a normal worry for the grandchildren.
S4.quote: Every loaf on your table had a bit of my shift in it, and one day a robot's shift instead.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Amira's retirement is safe and her husband's trade may do well during the change, so she's calmer than in any AGI picture. Her outlook stays family-centred and self-reliant. The image of potash in every loaf gave her job a dignity she clearly feels.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes both of us, me and Owen, before either of us is ready. What would help is the companies keeping older workers on to their pensions, and real apprenticeships so the young ones have somewhere to go. In our house we've always had one of us doing well when the other wasn't, and that's the bit the fast one takes away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask about the people who struggle with reading, like Dougie. Every change now comes with a screen and a test. Some of the best workers I know would fail the test and still be better at the job.

headlineQuote: In our house we've always had one of us doing well when the other wasn't, and that's the bit the fast one takes away.
portrait: Amira Evans is 58 and operates a continuous miner a kilometre underground at the Brightwater potash mine, part of a four-person panel crew she treats like family. Her husband Owen is a self-employed electrician, and after his van's gearbox went they have about three weeks of savings. She goes to chapel, minds grandchildren on her days off and uses AI now and then, checking it like a new worker. Steady and self-reliant, she's calm under hype and only uneasy under steady change, because Owen's trade might gain. AGI in two years alarms her because it would hit both incomes, while five and ten years let Owen earn during the change and her reach sixty-two.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would end both her job and her husband's electrical work before either is ready.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping older workers on until their pensions, and real apprenticeships for young people.
